title: Disaster at Cannae
objective: After this level you can explain what happened at Cannae and why it is still studied.
summary: At Cannae in 216 BCE Hannibal encircled a much larger Roman army and destroyed it. Rome lost tens of thousands, yet refused to make peace.

cards.headline: Rome’s biggest army walked into a trap it couldn’t escape.
The trap
cards.body: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal faced a much larger Roman army. He let the center of his line fall back as the Romans pushed forward. Then his wings and cavalry closed around them from both sides. It was a double envelopment.
cards.callout: Center falls back, wings close in

cards.headline: A catastrophe, and a refusal
cards.body: Ancient sources report Roman losses in the tens of thousands, one of the worst defeats in Roman history. Yet Rome refused to make peace. Hannibal had won a battle. He had not won the war, because Rome would not quit. Cannae is still studied as the classic example of encirclement.

cards.headline: Cannae: studied
learned: He encircled a larger Roman army
Rome still refused to make peace

questions.prompt: In what year was the Battle of Cannae?

options.label: 264 BCE
options.rationale: That’s when the Punic Wars began.

questions.explanation: Hannibal destroyed a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BCE.

questions.prompt: How did Hannibal defeat a larger army at Cannae?

options.label: He let his center give way, then closed in from both sides
He attacked the Roman camp at night
He used elephants to break the Roman line
options.rationale: The trap was about movement, not elephants.

questions.explanation: A retreating center drew the Romans in while the wings and cavalry surrounded them: a double envelopment.

questions.prompt: From Level 23: how had Hannibal’s army reached Italy before Cannae?

options.label: By a secret treaty with Rome
By marching over the Alps from Spain

questions.explanation: Hannibal crossed the Alps from Spain in 218 BCE, two years before Cannae.
